newsitem.title: UK: Market loves sterling but election upset looms.
newsitem.headline: Market loves sterling but election upset looms.

text.p: The market's love affair with sterling continues unabated despite a pending British general election and a growing view that interest rates will not rise this side of polling day.
During its strong advance since May last year there has been the occasional sell-off, although this tended to reflect profit-taking more than anything else, financial analysts said on Friday.
But they said an upset was on the way and that would come when Prime Minister John Major decided to call a general election, which must be held by May 22.
The assumption in the market is that Major will hold the election on May 1 and he has indicated that that would be his favourite date.
"Sterling is looking at bit toppish around here and all it's going to take is another political scare to knock it down," said Philip Uglow, economist at Union Plc.

This week sterling has put on nine pfennigs to flirt with the 2.71 mark level while against the dollar it has risen over three cents to $1.6325. Against the sliding yen it has hit its highest level since late 1992 at over 200 yen.

The continued strength has come despite disappointment in some quarters that Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George decided to leave interest rates on hold at their monthly monetary meeting this week.

The view in the market now is that the election date is so close that a rate rise would be politically unacceptable. While the central bank appears to have more say in monetary policy these days, it can still be overruled by the Treasury.
The prime minister is also First Lord of the Treasury so he could in theory overrule Clarke on any interest rate decision.

This was a problem with Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and her chancellor Nigel Lawson, who resigned over the fact he was being overruled. But in the case of Major and Clarke it is clear that currently Clarke makes the interest rate decisions, analysts said.

An opinion poll on Friday showed that the opposition Labour party's lead over the ruling Conservatives had edged down but they are still way ahead and are generally expected to form the next government.
"Sterling should come off again because the City still has a congenital anti-Labour bias and markets do get nervous ahead of an election," said Ian Amstad, International economist at Bankers Trust.
Post-election, as uncertainty is swept away, sterling will firm amid perceptions of tighter monetary policy.

Assuming a Labour victory, sterling would also be helped by Labour's perceived pro-European stance and the likelihood of the party being more friendly towards econmomic and monetary union (EMU) than the present administration.
"Labour are seen as being pro-European and more likely to take Britain into EMU at some stage," Union's Uglow said. "That will benefit sterling."
"There is a widespread expectation that any pre-election losses will be made up in the post-election period."
